    Reading Abaqus meshes with pyramids-mesh¶

    Abaqus (Dassault Systèmes) input decks (.inp) drive one of the most widely used finite-element solvers. They are keyword ASCII files: a *NODE block lists coordinates, and *ELEMENT, TYPE=... blocks list connectivity.

    Our sample uses TYPE=CPS3 — 3-node plane-stress triangles. Coordinates are in the model's engineering frame with no projection, so crs=None.

    We use nle1xf3c.inp: a small all-triangle plane-stress patch.

    Source: meshio test suite (tests/meshes/abaqus/), MIT.

    Imports¶

    The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

    In [1]:
    Copied! 
    import numpy as np
import geopandas as gpd
from pathlib import Path
from pyramids.netcdf.ugrid import MeshDataset

DATA = Path("../../examples/data")  # resolved relative to THIS notebook
DATA
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from cleopatra.basemap.tiles import add_tiles
    import numpy as np import geopandas as gpd from pathlib import Path from pyramids.netcdf.ugrid import MeshDataset DATA = Path("../../examples/data") # resolved relative to THIS notebook DATA import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from cleopatra.basemap.tiles import add_tiles

    Quickstart: read the Abaqus file¶

    driver="abaqus" parses the keyword grammar (*NODE / *ELEMENT).

    The one rule that matters: pass a pathlib.Path, never a str — read_file keys its driver dispatch off the Path type. MeshDataset.read_file(...) returns a MeshDataset, the in-memory UGRID container every pyramids-mesh driver produces.

    In [2]:
    Copied! 
    ds = MeshDataset.read_file(DATA / "abaqus" / "nle1xf3c.inp", driver="abaqus")
ds
    ds = MeshDataset.read_file(DATA / "abaqus" / "nle1xf3c.inp", driver="abaqus") ds

    What did we get?¶

    A few scalar properties describe the dataset at a glance: node and face counts, the coordinate reference system, and the planar bounding box.

    In [4]:
    Copied! 
    print("n_node :", ds.n_node)
print("n_face :", ds.n_face)
print("crs    :", ds.crs)
print("epsg   :", ds.epsg)
print("data   :", ds.data_variable_names)
print("bounds :", ds.bounds)
    print("n_node :", ds.n_node) print("n_face :", ds.n_face) print("crs :", ds.crs) print("epsg :", ds.epsg) print("data :", ds.data_variable_names) print("bounds :", ds.bounds)
    n_node : 12
n_face : 12
crs    : None
epsg   : None
data   : []
bounds : (0.0, 0.0, 3.25, 2.75)

    crs/epsg are None. There are no data variables — the deck is pure geometry. 12 nodes and 12 CPS3 triangles span a small 3.25×2.75 patch.

    Summary table¶

    ds.summary() returns a pandas DataFrame with per-variable statistics (count / min / max / mean / std). With no data variables the table is empty — confirming a geometry-only deck.

    In [5]:
    Copied! 
    ds.summary()
    ds.summary()
    Out[5]:
    count min max mean std
    variable

    The mesh geometry¶

    ds.mesh is a Mesh2d: node coordinates plus the face-node connectivity, an (n_face, k) integer table where k is the largest number of nodes any face has. Triangles fill 3 columns; quadrilaterals fill 4 (a shorter face pads the spare slot). face_areas and face_centroids are derived on demand.

    In [6]:
    Copied! 
    mesh = ds.mesh
fnc = mesh.face_node_connectivity.data
areas = mesh.face_areas
cx, cy = mesh.face_centroids
print("mesh type         :", type(mesh).__name__)
print("connectivity shape:", fnc.shape)
print("node_x range      :", float(mesh.node_x.min()), "->", float(mesh.node_x.max()))
print("node_y range      :", float(mesh.node_y.min()), "->", float(mesh.node_y.max()))
print("face_areas        :", float(areas.min()), "->", float(areas.max()))
print("centroids shape   :", (cx.shape, cy.shape))
    mesh = ds.mesh fnc = mesh.face_node_connectivity.data areas = mesh.face_areas cx, cy = mesh.face_centroids print("mesh type :", type(mesh).__name__) print("connectivity shape:", fnc.shape) print("node_x range :", float(mesh.node_x.min()), "->", float(mesh.node_x.max())) print("node_y range :", float(mesh.node_y.min()), "->", float(mesh.node_y.max())) print("face_areas :", float(areas.min()), "->", float(areas.max())) print("centroids shape :", (cx.shape, cy.shape))
    mesh type         : Mesh2d
connectivity shape: (12, 3)
node_x range      : 0.0 -> 3.25
node_y range      : 0.0 -> 2.75
face_areas        : 0.1415624840625 -> 0.7800625481250001
centroids shape   : ((12,), (12,))

    The connectivity is (12, 3): 12 triangles, three nodes each — the CPS3 elements. Areas vary across the patch, so the elements are not uniform.

    Wireframe¶

    plot_outline() draws the bare mesh edges — the quickest way to eyeball the topology and the element shapes before colouring anything.

    In [7]:
    Copied! 
    _g = ds.plot_outline()
if ds.epsg:
    add_tiles(_g.ax, crs=ds.epsg)
plt.title("Abaqus mesh outline")
    _g = ds.plot_outline() if ds.epsg: add_tiles(_g.ax, crs=ds.epsg) plt.title("Abaqus mesh outline")
    Out[7]:
    Text(0.5, 1.0, 'Abaqus mesh outline')

    A derived field: cell area¶

    These engineering files usually carry no cell data we can colour by — so we compute one ourselves. with_variable attaches face_areas as a face-located variable, giving a non-destructive copy of the dataset that plot can render as a filled colour map.

    In [8]:
    Copied! 
    d2 = ds.with_variable("cell_area", ds.mesh.face_areas, location="face")
_g = d2.plot("cell_area", cmap="viridis", colorbar=True, title="Abaqus — cell area")
if ds.epsg:
    add_tiles(_g.ax, crs=ds.epsg)
    d2 = ds.with_variable("cell_area", ds.mesh.face_areas, location="face") _g = d2.plot("cell_area", cmap="viridis", colorbar=True, title="Abaqus — cell area") if ds.epsg: add_tiles(_g.ax, crs=ds.epsg)

    The colour map shows the graded triangle sizes across the plane-stress patch — finer where the analyst wanted resolution.

    Treating the mesh as GIS¶

    Because a MeshDataset is just nodes and polygonal faces, pyramids exposes the usual vector-GIS toolbox on it. First, every face as a GeoPandas polygon:

    In [9]:
    Copied! 
    gdf = ds.to_geodataframe()
print(type(gdf).__name__, gdf.shape)
gdf.head()
    gdf = ds.to_geodataframe() print(type(gdf).__name__, gdf.shape) gdf.head()
    GeoDataFrame (12, 1)
    Out[9]:
    geometry
    0 POLYGON ((1.474 1.55602, 0 1.875, 0 1, 1.474 1...
    1 POLYGON ((0 1, 1.165 0.81283, 1.474 1.55602, 0...
    2 POLYGON ((2.30791 0.9005, 1.474 1.55602, 1.165...
    3 POLYGON ((1.165 0.81283, 1.78302 0.453, 2.3079...
    4 POLYGON ((2.625 0, 2.30791 0.9005, 1.78302 0.4...

    Being a real GeoDataFrame, it plots with GeoPandas directly — a filled view of every element footprint:

    In [10]:
    Copied! 
    ax = gdf.plot(edgecolor="black", linewidth=0.3, facecolor="#cfe8ff")
if ds.epsg:
    add_tiles(ax, crs=ds.epsg)
plt.title("Abaqus faces as polygons"); plt.gca().set_aspect("equal")
    ax = gdf.plot(edgecolor="black", linewidth=0.3, facecolor="#cfe8ff") if ds.epsg: add_tiles(ax, crs=ds.epsg) plt.title("Abaqus faces as polygons"); plt.gca().set_aspect("equal")

    The outer boundary¶

    bounding_polygon() dissolves the triangles into the patch outline.

    In [11]:
    Copied! 
    poly = ds.bounding_polygon()
print("geometry type:", poly.geom_type)
ax = gpd.GeoSeries([poly]).plot(facecolor="none", edgecolor="red", linewidth=2)
if ds.epsg:
    add_tiles(ax, crs=ds.epsg)
plt.gca().set_aspect("equal"); plt.title("bounding polygon")
    poly = ds.bounding_polygon() print("geometry type:", poly.geom_type) ax = gpd.GeoSeries([poly]).plot(facecolor="none", edgecolor="red", linewidth=2) if ds.epsg: add_tiles(ax, crs=ds.epsg) plt.gca().set_aspect("equal"); plt.title("bounding polygon")
    geometry type: Polygon
    Out[11]:
    Text(0.5, 1.0, 'bounding polygon')

    Cropping to a bounding box¶

    crop(bbox=...) returns a new MeshDataset with only the faces inside the box — handy for zooming into a region of a large mesh. We crop to the left half of the extent.

    In [12]:
    Copied! 
    xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax = ds.bounds
half = ds.crop(bbox=(xmin, ymin, (xmin + xmax) / 2, ymax))
print("faces before / after:", ds.n_face, "->", half.n_face)
half.plot_outline(); plt.title("cropped to the left half")
    xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax = ds.bounds half = ds.crop(bbox=(xmin, ymin, (xmin + xmax) / 2, ymax)) print("faces before / after:", ds.n_face, "->", half.n_face) half.plot_outline(); plt.title("cropped to the left half")
    faces before / after: 12 -> 4
    Out[12]:
    Text(0.5, 1.0, 'cropped to the left half')

    The face-adjacency graph¶

    sparse_adjacency() gives the face-to-face adjacency as a SciPy sparse matrix, and connected_components() labels which faces are reachable from which. plt.spy shows the sparsity pattern — the fingerprint of how the faces are wired together.

    In [13]:
    Copied! 
    adj = ds.sparse_adjacency()
comp = ds.connected_components()
print("adjacency:", adj.shape, "nnz =", adj.nnz)
print("connected components:", np.unique(comp).size)
plt.spy(adj, markersize=0.6); plt.title("face adjacency")
    adj = ds.sparse_adjacency() comp = ds.connected_components() print("adjacency:", adj.shape, "nnz =", adj.nnz) print("connected components:", np.unique(comp).size) plt.spy(adj, markersize=0.6); plt.title("face adjacency")
    adjacency: (12, 12) nnz = 26
connected components: 1
    Out[13]:
    Text(0.5, 1.0, 'face adjacency')

    The triangles form one connected patch (a single component); the spy plot shows each interior triangle linked to its edge neighbours.

    A triangle-only operation: circumcenters¶

    Every CPS3 element is a triangle, so circumcenters() is defined. We overlay the circumcenters (red) on the area-weighted centroids (blue) — note how they diverge for the more skewed triangles.

    In [14]:
    Copied! 
    cc = ds.circumcenters()
cx, cy = ds.mesh.face_centroids
_g = ds.plot_outline()
if ds.epsg:
    add_tiles(_g.ax, crs=ds.epsg)
plt.scatter(cx, cy, c="blue", label="centroid")
plt.scatter(cc[0], cc[1], c="red", marker="x", label="circumcenter")
plt.legend(); plt.title("centroids vs circumcenters")
    cc = ds.circumcenters() cx, cy = ds.mesh.face_centroids _g = ds.plot_outline() if ds.epsg: add_tiles(_g.ax, crs=ds.epsg) plt.scatter(cx, cy, c="blue", label="centroid") plt.scatter(cc[0], cc[1], c="red", marker="x", label="circumcenter") plt.legend(); plt.title("centroids vs circumcenters")
    Out[14]:
    Text(0.5, 1.0, 'centroids vs circumcenters')

    Converting out: other drivers¶

    to_file(path, driver=...) re-serialises the mesh through any writer in the driver table — here a round-trip to the 2dm format in a temp file.

    In [15]:
    Copied! 
    import tempfile
out = Path(tempfile.gettempdir()) / "abaqus_roundtrip.2dm"
ds.to_file(out, driver="2dm")
print("wrote:", out.name, "| exists:", out.exists())
    import tempfile out = Path(tempfile.gettempdir()) / "abaqus_roundtrip.2dm" ds.to_file(out, driver="2dm") print("wrote:", out.name, "| exists:", out.exists())
    wrote: abaqus_roundtrip.2dm | exists: True

    What we cannot do here: reprojection & regridding¶

    to_crs(epsg) reprojects between coordinate systems — but this mesh has crs=None (model-local coordinates, no datum), so there is nothing to reproject from; we skip it. Likewise rasterize_like(...) and regrid(...) map a data field onto a raster or another mesh; with no meaningful field and no georeferencing on an engineering mesh they are out of scope. These belong on georeferenced hydrodynamic meshes, not FEM/CFD decks.

    Note — xarray interop. pyramids-core exposes a to_xarray() bridge to the xarray ecosystem, but these notebooks deliberately stay within pyramids-core's own GDAL-based UGRID I/O and do not use xarray.

    Takeaway¶

    • driver="abaqus" reads a keyword .inp deck (*NODE + *ELEMENT TYPE=CPS3) into a MeshDataset.
    • An all-triangle plane-stress patch, geometry-only (crs=None, no data variables).
    • All GIS operations work, and because it is triangular, circumcenters does too.
    • No CRS → reprojection and regridding do not apply.
